headline: A New Genus of Bugs Bears Taylor Swift's Name
meta_description: Scientists at UC Riverside named a new genus of Australian plant bugs after Taylor Swift, honoring her talent and the joy she brings to millions.
summary_short: Researchers have named a new genus of Australian plant bugs Swiftiephylus, with four species honoring Taylor Swift and her albums.
body:
Scientists at the University of California, Riverside have formally described a new genus of plant bugs and named it Swiftiephylus—in honor of Grammy-winning singer Taylor Swift. The genus contains 12 new species, four of which directly reference the artist: Swiftiephylus taylorae (a Latinized version of Taylor), along with species named after her albums "Lover," "Fearless," and "The Tortured Poets Department." According to the study, the naming recognizes Swift's "show-stopping talent, heart-wrenching lyrics, and the joy and comfort she has brought to many," while also celebrating her fanbase, known as Swifties.

Study author Sarah Schroeder, herself a Swiftie, drew inspiration from Swift's iconic appearance. "Taylor Swift's signature look is her blonde hair and red lips," Schroeder explained. "These insects are pale yellow with accents of red throughout." The coloring serves a practical purpose: it helps the bugs camouflage among the spindly red and orange flowers they inhabit on Australian trees and shrubs. Swiftiephylus plant bugs belong to the Miridae family, the largest family of true bugs, which contains over 11,000 described species worldwide. These particular specimens were collected between 1995 and 2004 from museum collections.

The decision to name insects after celebrities may seem unconventional, but experts argue it serves science well. Akito Kawahara, director of the McGuire Center for Lepidoptera and Biodiversity in Florida, notes that such naming draws crucial attention to insects—organisms that often go overlooked despite their ecological importance. With many insect species disappearing and facing extinction, the celebrity connection can inspire public interest in biodiversity conservation and environmental protection.
quick_facts: UC Riverside scientists named a new bug genus Swiftiephylus after Taylor Swift
Four of the 12 species reference Swift's albums and her Latinized name
The pale yellow insects with red accents live on Australian plants
Museum specimens collected between 1995 and 2004 were formally described
